FR-001.title: Every heat number and supplier combination gets exactly one shape and color.

FR-002.title: The system chooses the marking, not the user.

FR-003.title: The same heat number and supplier always resolve to the same marking.

FR-004.title: A marking is fixed on first sight and never changes.

FR-005.title: The same heat number from two suppliers produces two markings.

FR-006.title: Supplier identity comes from the official supplier record.

FR-007.title: Receipts with no supplier share one common group.

FR-008.title: A blank heat number gets no marking and blocks nothing.

FR-009.title: Only enabled part numbers receive markings.

FR-010.title: Parts off the list stay fully receivable.

FR-011.title: Parts are added to the list by searching, not by typing from memory.

FR-012.title: Removing a part leaves existing markings unchanged.

FR-013.title: One system-wide switch turns the feature off without deleting markings.

FR-014.title: Each receipt line and each receipt shows its lots shapes and colors.

FR-015.title: A lot colliding with an active lot gets a different marking automatically.

FR-016.title: Markings survive history promotion and reprint.

FR-017.title: Markings can be found by heat number search.

FR-018.title: A user can replace a marking by hand with a recorded reason.

FR-019.title: A locked marking is never changed by the system.

FR-020.title: Manual changes record who and when.

FR-021.title: The full shape and color set is visible in the tool.

FR-022.title: Tool access is limited to Ship-Rec Tools users.

decisions.decision: A lot is identified by the pair (normalized heat number, supplier group).
decisions.why: Two suppliers using the same heat number must stay visually distinct, and the receipt tables store the supplier as a name only.
decisions.rejected: Keying on the heat number alone, or on heat plus part number, either merges two suppliers or splits one physical lot.

decisions.decision: The hash is only a seed; the ledger row is authoritative once written.
decisions.why: A live recompute would repaint every historical lot when a shape or color is added later, while the physical marking cannot change.
decisions.rejected: Pure recompute with no ledger, or a cache-only ledger rebuilt on demand.

decisions.decision: Collisions are resolved by a bounded deterministic probe against other live markings, with the policy exposed as a setting.
decisions.why: 156 combinations collide about 70 percent of the time once twenty lots are active, and the ledger already holds what the probe needs.
decisions.rejected: Ignoring collisions, or adding a fill-pattern dimension before the need is proven.

decisions.decision: The marking is resolved once at save time and copied verbatim through promotion and reprint, never recomputed.
decisions.why: Promotion and reprint happen later than the receipt, so a recompute would disagree with what the handler saw, and reprint rows never re-resolve.
decisions.rejected: Resolving lazily at display time, or resolving again at promotion.

decisions.decision: A heat number counts as blank when it is null, empty, whitespace only, or the literal string the receiving flow substitutes for blank.
decisions.why: Blank heat values are stored as that literal, so treating it as a real lot would collapse every blank-heat line into one shared lot.
decisions.rejected: Treating only null and whitespace as blank, or removing the sentinel at its source.

decisions.decision: A dedicated normalizer builds the matching key and the stored heat value is left untouched.
decisions.why: The key must collapse separators and casing, but existing rows and the reprint procedure copy the stored value verbatim.

decisions.decision: The supplier is resolved from the receipt's name to the official supplier id, falling back to the normalized name, and the non-supplier group uses the literal sentinel.
decisions.why: The official record must be authoritative, but only a fuzzy vendor search exists, and a unique key cannot hold a NULL without permitting duplicates.
decisions.rejected: Comparing normalized names only, or failing the receipt when the supplier cannot be resolved.

decisions.decision: The enabled part list is a table with a unique key and an active flag, and removal deactivates rather than deletes.
decisions.why: It is data rather than a preference, and the active flag satisfies the requirement that removal leaves recorded markings untouched.
decisions.rejected: A JSON settings value, or hard deletion on removal.

decisions.decision: New settings join the existing ShipRecTools category, and only the system-wide switch is gated above a normal user.
decisions.why: The category needs no parser change, and a missing manifest entry fails closed, so under-permissioning is the safe direction.
decisions.rejected: Making every key user level, or creating a new settings category.

decisions.decision: The marking shows on each receipt line, on the per-step receipt header, and in the reprint grid.
decisions.why: The reprint grid is where a reprinted receipt is reviewed, and its mapper currently discards the heat value the procedure already returns.
decisions.rejected: Receipt lines only, which fails the receipt-level requirement.

decisions.decision: The schema change ships as both a numbered schema file and a migration, and the migration re-creates the receiving procedures it invalidates.
decisions.why: Schema files use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and cannot alter an installed database, and the affected procedures enumerate their columns explicitly.
decisions.rejected: Migration only, schema files only, or relying on a separate procedure re-deployment.

decisions.decision: The manual override records an explicit change reason separate from the operator notes field.
decisions.why: A reason is required and must be queryable, which free-text notes cannot provide.
decisions.rejected: Overloading the notes column, or adding a separate audit table.

decisions.decision: The four write procedures (sp_Receiving_LabelData_Insert, sp_Receiving_LabelData_Update, sp_Receiving_Load_Insert, sp_Receiving_Load_Update) keep their current signatures until the receiving row model and queue DAO change lands with them.
decisions.why: MySQL stored procedures do not support default parameter values, so adding the two marking parameters now would break every existing caller with an incorrect-argument-count error until the DAO passes them.
decisions.rejected: Adding the parameters immediately and leaving the receiving workflow broken until the DAO change lands.

decisions.decision: The shape vocabulary is emoji only, and the emoji itself is the value persisted in shape_code and heat_shape_code.
decisions.why: The shape must render on screen and be stored as the same thing, so the drawn value and the stored value can never drift apart, and no mapping layer can fall out of step.
decisions.rejected: Keeping abstract name codes and mapping them to emoji at display time.

decisions.decision: Enum_LotShape was deleted, and the palette split into Model_LotMarkingShape (Glyph, DisplayName, SortOrder) and Model_LotMarkingColor (Code, DisplayName, HexToken, SortOrder).
decisions.why: With the glyph as the value, an enum of name codes is dead and misleading, and a shape carries no hex token because the emoji brings its own colour.
decisions.rejected: Leaving the enum in place as a record of the old vocabulary.

decisions.decision: The property stays named ShapeCode and the column stays named shape_code, with the XML documentation stating that it holds the emoji.
decisions.why: The property mirrors its column name, which is the convention elsewhere in this module, and renaming a column nobody asked to rename is churn.
decisions.rejected: Renaming the property to ShapeGlyph, which would break the column-mirroring convention used across the module.

decisions.decision: Core was deployed only after the test database proved the same ordered manifest, a backup was taken, and the procedures were smoke tested.
decisions.why: The seven re-deployed receiving procedures are the only change that touches existing behaviour, and the running build calls them.
decisions.rejected: Applying to core first and verifying afterwards, which would have risked the running build the deployment had to protect.

decisions.decision: The sync policy admits lot_marking_part_scope as reference data and excludes lot_markings, because the ledger key is heat plus supplier and copying rows would collide and replace a marking a handler has already seen

The settings page view and view model are registered in DI although the task named only three registration sites, because the settings search path resolves the page from the container and GetService returns null when it is missing
The palette row type for the settings page lives inside the settings view model file rather than a new Models file, because the task file list did not include one
Shape and color render as text, the glyph itself and the color code, because the repository has no hex to brush converter and adding one was outside scope
The collision policy is read from settings by the receiving caller and passed to the resolver, because the already built service takes it as an argument

T045 was unblocked with a new shared ViewModel_Receiving_StepBase for the four guided-step view models, rather than adding a receiving concept to ViewModel_Shared_Base and so to every view model in the application
The receipt header card binds one joined line, ReceiptLotMarkingsText, instead of an item template, because a one-line display does not justify a DataTemplate and its x:DataType dependency

The 21 objects the catalog regeneration dropped are retired rather than lost: migration 13 retired dunnage_specs and its procedures, and no matching SQL files remain, so the committed catalog was stale
The docs/database reference pages were not written because the repository contains no generator for them; they are hand-authored HTML over a curated subset of tables

specify.summary: 60 tasks across Setup, Foundational, five user-story phases and Polish, with the tool page and its wiring placed in Foundational because two stories would otherwise share those files.
specify.key_finding: The receiving flow stores a blank heat number as the literal string Nothing Entered, so the resolver must treat that value as blank or every blank-heat line in the application would collapse into one shared lot.

implement.summary: Heat / Lot Management shipped: two tables with eleven procedures plus the additive SetMarking procedure, the tool page and its settings page fully wired, markings resolved once on the receiving save path and copied verbatim through promotion and reprint, and twenty new tests. Two tasks remain open: the per-step receipt header card and the regenerated SQL object catalog.

approach: Give every unique heat number and supplier pair a permanent shape-and-color marking. The marking is pinned in a new ledger table on first sight, written onto the receiving queue row, and copied verbatim through promotion and reprint. Only part numbers on an enabled list receive markings, maintained from a new settings page that reuses the existing fuzzy-search picker.

concerns.note: The palette carries a text glyph only for the shapes that have a dependable Unicode character; the remaining shapes show their display name. A dedicated shape icon set is the next step for the marking display.

T018 is partly complete: seven of the eleven procedures are updated, and the four write procedures are deliberately deferred to land with T035 and T036 so the receiving workflow never breaks in between.

The shape set fell from 13 to 10, so the combination space dropped from 156 to 120 and accidental collisions become slightly more likely. The probe policy absorbs it, but it is a real reduction in distinct markings.

An emoji brings its own colour, so a marking now shows two colour signals: the emoji and the colour swatch. The two can disagree in tone, and the red cross or red circle emoji will never match a blue lot colour.
Shape code length is now variable because some emoji are two code points, so shape_code and heat_shape_code must remain at least VARCHAR(32) and the column must stay utf8mb4 to hold them.
